title: National Nutritional Foods Association v. Kennedy
lead: Congress sharply limited the supplement regulations being reconsidered after an earlier remand. The Food and Drug Administration treated its response as implementation needing no new participation, but the court found meaningful remaining choices and required notice and comment.

actors.name: Food and Drug Administration and Commissioner Kennedy
actors.role: Regulator and respondent defending reissued supplement rules

actors.name: Manufacturers and trade associations
actors.role: Petitioners seeking public participation and substantive corrections

actors.name: Dr. Miles Robinson
actors.role: Individual petitioner challenging allowance evidence and rules

actors.name: Dr. Alfred Harper
actors.role: Successor witness at the reopened scientific hearing

actors.name: Judge Friendly
actors.role: Author of the unanimous appellate opinion

proceedings: Following the 1974 remand, a reopened hearing, and 1976 legislation, the FDA issued final rules without participation on the statute. On February 16, 1978, the Second Circuit vacated and remanded while resolving additional issues to guide the agency.
limits: The court required informal notice and comment, not another unrestricted trial-type hearing. It sustained certain unchanged conclusions and safety authority while reserving matters for the new statutory proceeding.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An earlier remand left specific tasks for the agency
sections.cue: Connect this case to the preceding regulatory litigation.
paragraphs: The Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, began supplement regulation in 1962, generating twenty-two months of hearings and 32,405 transcript pages. In National Nutritional Foods Association v. FDA in 1974, the Second Circuit broadly upheld identity standards but stayed enforcement and required meaningful combination and dosage exceptions, relief for essential nutrients without allowances, removal of automatic high-dose drug classification, qualified iron labeling, exemption of natural fresh produce, and reopened questioning of a key allowances witness.

In May 1975, the FDA invited formulation applications, proposed amendments, and reopened the hearing, allowing higher-dose single nutrients without special applications. Because Dr. Sebrell no longer belonged to the Food and Nutrition Board, successor chair Dr. Alfred Harper testified about scientific methodology, regulatory use of allowances, and bias. Six days in November added 1,119 pages. The administrative law judge found no demonstrated bias affecting judgment, regarded the allowances as sound, and found no need to alter the rules after detailed questioning. Parties filed exceptions.

sections.title: Congress changed the program’s legal foundation
sections.cue: Describe the new limits and remaining authority.
paragraphs: On April 22, 1976, Public Law 94-278 added section 411. For covered special-dietary foods it generally prohibited maximum-potency limits under identified provisions, drug classification solely for allegedly irrational or useless potency, and limits on ingredient combinations or numbers. Exceptions preserved authority over disease-treatment or management representations, children under twelve, and pregnant or lactating women.

Labeling authority was less restricted. Ingredients could not be wholly suppressed just for being neither vitamins nor minerals, though prominence and presentation remained regulable. Section 501(b) expressly required amendments implementing the new law to use Administrative Procedure Act section 553.

Without further participation on the legislation, the FDA issued October 19 final rules largely readopting its reorganized scheme with an exemption for restrictions Congress forbade. It treated almost all formulation requests as moot, approved one infant-and-child combination, rejected higher B6 for pregnant or lactating women, classified estrogen-containing multinutrient products for oral-contraceptive users as drugs, and added a food-additive provision. It also rejected challenges to Harper’s examination and the proposed amendments.

sections.title: An urgent petition challenged the lack of participation
paragraphs: Manufacturers and associations petitioned urgently on November 30 for withdrawal and a new proposed order. The agency answered only in April 1977, asserting good cause because Congress had already dictated the changes and rejecting renewed formal hearings. The rules were later postponed to July 1, 1979. Manufacturers, associations, and Dr. Miles Robinson sought appellate review.

Judge Friendly, joined by Judges Smith and Meskill, found that Congress plainly addressed this nutrition program despite the earlier enforcement stay. The FDA did not rely on a literal claim that stayed rules were outside the amendment direction; it argued section 553’s exceptions accompanied the congressional reference. The court accepted that general proposition but found no applicable exception.

sections.title: Substantial remaining choices defeated good cause
sections.cue: Give the procedural holding and its limits.
paragraphs: The final rule lacked an adequate good-cause finding and explanation. Saying rules had been revised in recognition of Congress explained the action, not omission of public participation. Belated justification was suspect, though the court reserved whether reconsideration could ever supply one. These reasons failed even if timely.

Impracticability, unnecessary procedure, and public interest were narrow exceptions. Fourteen years of proceedings and the agency’s extended stay showed no emergency. Congress had removed powers, added labeling duties, and left choices about regulating the remaining disease-related, child, and pregnancy categories. Evidence supporting a universal identity scheme might not justify the narrowed one. This was a new regulatory judgment, not technical deletion of forbidden words, and the urgent petition demonstrated public interest.

Notice and comment was required, but Congress selected section 553 rather than the previous formal procedure. The FDA need not reopen issues previously available but unraised, rejected without appeal, or already resolved in its favor unless the legislation gave them a significantly new aspect. Many objections remained for that proceeding.

sections.title: The old scientific findings and minimum limits did not all disappear
sections.cue: Separate settled issues from new applications.
paragraphs: Robinson’s renewed attacks on Harper’s bias, hearing rulings, and general allowance methodology failed insofar as they repeated the old issue. Yet participation was needed on whether allowances suited the three categories still subject to maxima and combinations. Rejecting old methodology objections did not approve every new use.

Minimum-potency limits survived because the conference report expressly preserved protection against uselessly small ingredients. Petitioners accused the agency of shifting from confusion to nutritional significance without evidence, but earlier findings already addressed insignificant amounts and impractical numbers of units needed for usefulness. Supplements differed from individual components of ordinary meals. The court adhered to its earlier approval of minima.

sections.title: Several corrections remained incomplete
sections.cue: Explain essential nutrients, exceptions, and labeling.
paragraphs: The FDA still had not justified excluding essential nutrients lacking allowances from standardized combinations. Allowing them in newly exempt products did not comply with the earlier direction, and repeating that ordinary diets were not deficient supplied no new basis. The agency could develop evidence in the changed statutory setting rather than mechanically follow old directions despite a supported new justification.

The variance standard also improperly required proof of greater honesty and fair dealing than the existing rule. A proposal should qualify if it achieved those objectives equally, including as knowledge advanced; the agency need not recite every previously listed factor.

The iron proviso said conventional food often made adequate supply impractical, implying that an obtainable balanced diet would suffice. Prior evidence showed difficulty even with such a diet for infants, children, and childbearing-age women. Without contrary evidence the real qualification had to be implemented. New testimony did not support comparable relief for B6, folic acid, or magnesium. A vitamin K distinction also did not require rewriting the general natural-versus-synthetic rule for listed nutrients, though individual relief remained possible.

sections.title: Safety-based additive regulation remained permissible
sections.cue: State the sustained power and final vacatur.
paragraphs: Petitioners argued food-additive regulation would recreate forbidden potency limits. The new provision applied where qualified experts did not generally recognize safety under intended conditions, invoking approval requirements. Petitioners conceded power over dangerous potency but preferred ordinary adulteration proceedings.

The court found no categorical incompatibility between food and food additive: a food could become another food’s component without generally recognized safety. Text, public-health purposes, and rulemaking authority supported that reading. The 1976 materials preserved additive regulation for potentially toxic ingredients while rejecting its use merely to enforce disfavored potency or combination preferences. Section 105.85(f) was not infirm, without making every high-dose supplement unsafe or an additive. Petitioners had received participation on that provision; invalidated cross-references were assumed removed, and untimely collateral attacks were declined.

An objection to guaranteeing labeled potency at expiration without tolerance also came too late because it was available in the prior review, although the agency could voluntarily consider it. Despite these agency victories, the final judgment vacated the regulations and remanded to the Commissioner on February 16, 1978. No judge wrote separately.
